item.title: Finance Pulse - Aug 31, 2026
item.description:
I'll run all key searches simultaneously to capture the freshest developments as of Monday, August 31, 2026.Now let me run one final targeted search for the August jobs report and any fresh super-regional bank news this morning.I now have all the material I need. The August jobs report (for August, releasing today, Monday August 31) is the forward catalyst the market is watching. The July report showed payrolls fell by 23,000 and prior months were revised down by a combined 103,000, with financial activities losing 14,000 jobs. Today's August NFP is the single data point that could either confirm or undercut Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole stance and determine whether September's FOMC produces a hike. Let me synthesize both parts.
---
## Finance Pulse | Monday, August 31, 2026
**Bottom line: Warsh's unexpectedly hawkish Jackson Hole speech has reset the September hike probability to roughly sixty percent on CME FedWatch as of this morning, up from thirty-six percent pre-speech, and the August jobs number dropping today is now the single most consequential data release of the year for bank CFO planning assumptions -- but the underappreciated story entering this week is not the rate path itself: it is the compounding asymmetry now facing bank finance functions, where a hike would arrest the deposit cost relief that has barely begun, a weak jobs print would re-open cut expectations, and Warsh's deliberate refusal to provide forward guidance leaves CFOs holding a planning scenario set wider than at any point in this cycle.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech was unexpectedly hawkish, and traders of fed funds futures now see a sixty point four percent chance of a quarter-point hike in September, up from around fifty-six percent on Friday.
2. Warsh cited a specific internal inflation metric: fifty-four percent of PCE components had been above three percent annualized inflation in the past twelve months, and forty-nine percent above three percent in the past six months -- figures he described as an indication the Fed may need to raise rates.
3. The government's next price report, to be released just days before the September sixteen meeting, could play an outsize role in determining whether the central bank acts -- and today's August jobs report is the first of those deciding data points.
4. July payrolls unexpectedly declined by twenty-three thousand, while the unemployment rate edged lower to four point one percent largely because of a further decline in labor force participation. A repeat or worse today would materially complicate the hike case.
5. Although the March 2026 Basel III re-proposals may relieve certain capital pressures, the 2026 capital rules also add complexity and will require careful implementation, and banks will need to reassess internal models, governance frameworks, and capital planning processes.
6. Close to sixty percent of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects, while only seven percent of CFOs say those investments are having a strong impact -- the ROI gap is now the defining finance technology debate.
---
### Key Themes
**Theme 1 (New): The Warsh "Deliberate Opacity" Hike Premium and Today's Jobs Test**
The post-Jackson Hole story is not the hawkish tilt in isolation -- it is the combinatorial planning burden it creates. Though Warsh doubled down on his controversial refusal to provide forward guidance on Fed moves, a majority of investors now expect a rate hike in September. Warsh recommitted to the Fed's two percent PCE inflation target, said elevated prices should be the central bank's main focus, and confirmed short-term interest rates remain the primary tool -- a speech that puts him more clearly at odds with White House demands for lower rates and raises the stakes for the September meeting. For CFOs running NII sensitivity analyses, the no-forward-guidance posture means the probability distribution across September outcomes is wider today than it was after any prior FOMC communication in this cycle.
**Theme 2 (Evolving): Basel III Endgame Comment Period Closed -- Now a Compliance Workload, Not a Policy Debate**
After nearly three years of controversy, on March nineteenth, 2026, the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC issued three proposals that would comprehensively overhaul the existing U.S. bank capital framework and implement the Basel III endgame. Comments on all three proposals were due by June eighteenth, 2026. With the comment period closed, this story has shifted from regulatory lobbying to implementation planning. The Fed, OCC, and FDIC now project that aggregate capital in the banking system will modestly decrease under the new framework -- a dramatic pivot from the original plus-sixteen percent CET1 increase -- but for operational risk managers, internal models are still gone, the Standardized Approach is still coming, and the compliance clock is ticking. The finance transformation angle: banks above the one-hundred billion dollar threshold now face a mandatory rebuild of capital calculation methodology that runs directly through the controller and treasury functions.
**Theme 3 (New): The Agentic AI ROI Gap -- Where Finance Budgets Are Shifting Despite the Hype Penalty**
NVIDIA's 2026 State of AI in Financial Services report found that forty-two percent of respondents are already using or assessing agentic AI, especially for internal process optimization, task orchestration, and regulatory compliance or risk monitoring. Yet close to sixty percent of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects while only seven percent of CFOs report strong impact, with the gap stemming from architectural limitations -- most finance teams are adding AI inside existing functional lanes. The practical implication for bank finance transformation: spend is real but siloed. AI agents can automate variance analysis with driver attribution, recurring forecasting, anomaly detection on people costs and revenue, routine close tasks, and standard board reporting -- but only where the data plumbing is already clean. Banks with fragmented GL and ERP architectures are discovering that the AI investment surfaces the data modernization deficit more than it solves it.
---
### Banking Finance-Function
**NIM and Rate Sensitivity -- New Asymmetry from Today's Jobs Print**
The August analysis of Q2 PrecisionLender commercial loan and deposit pricing data looks at July 2026 activity, and for the first time in several months the picture is broadly positive: spreads expanded across all three rate structures, coupons rose in tandem, and NIM improved on both fixed and floating deals -- notably July marked the first month to reverse a fixed-rate spread narrowing that had persisted since January. But the Federal Reserve cut short-term rates by seventy-five basis points last fall, and deposit rates in the PrecisionLender portfolio have not followed that move lower -- at least not by anything close to that magnitude. A September hike would arrest even the modest deposit cost relief that has begun to materialize.
**Labor Market Signal for Financial Activities** In July, employment in financial activities declined by fourteen thousand -- a quiet but direct signal that the sector's own headcount is under pressure, which directly reshapes the make-versus-buy calculus for finance transformation vendors pitching managed services and automation.
**Capital Planning -- From Optionality to Complexity** Overall bank capital requirements are expected to decrease across the industry due to lower minimum risk weights and less conservative methodologies, improving capital efficiency and bringing regulatory capital into closer alignment with actual risk. But the lighter headline capital burden does not reduce planning complexity. The structural shift from internal models to the Standardized Approach for operational risk remains intact, and every bank above the one-hundred billion dollar threshold must prepare for a fundamentally different methodology regardless of whether aggregate capital requirements go up or down.
---
### Regulatory Radar
The Basel III re-proposal comment period closed June eighteenth. The rule is now in finalization mode, with Bloomberg Intelligence projecting a final rule in late 2026 and implementation beginning in 2027. The agencies anticipate that the amount of overall capital in the banking system would modestly decrease if the proposals are implemented, though levels would remain substantially higher than pre-crisis; the FRB voted six to one to advance all three proposals, with Governor Barr as the sole dissenting vote.
The FOMC September sixteenth meeting will include updated dot plots and a Summary of Economic Projections -- the first SEP under Warsh -- which creates an additional scenario-planning obligation for bank treasurers that has no precedent in recent cycles.
---
### AI in Finance
**The Adoption-Impact Gap is the New Headline**
Gartner predicts ninety percent of finance functions will deploy at least one AI-enabled technology solution by 2026, yet close to sixty percent of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects while only seven percent of CFOs say those investments are having strong impact. This gap is the defining commercial dynamic for finance technology vendors right now -- and it is creating a purchasing pattern shift: banks are moving away from point-solution pilots toward platform consolidation bids. PwC's 2026 Digital Trends in Operations Survey found that eighty-three percent of respondents believe AI agents and automation will accelerate the breakdown of traditional functional silos, yet only twenty-seven percent have fully embedded an AI strategy.
**Oracle Move into Treasury and Trade Finance** Oracle Financial Services extended its agentic AI platform to corporate banking in April 2026, releasing pre-built AI agents for treasury, trade finance, credit, and lending that automate mission-critical processes and speed decision-making to help banks navigate market volatility and risk. This is a named vendor deployment -- not marketing -- and it signals that the platform incumbents are now competing directly on treasury and risk workflow automation, territory previously owned by specialist vendors.
**Workforce Signal** The 2026 FP&A Trends Survey found that forty-seven percent of FP&A time is now spent on data collection and validation, the highest figure in five years -- and that is exactly the type of work that agentic AI thrives in: high-effort, low-judgment, and repetitive. For bank CFOs navigating falling finance headcount alongside rising regulatory workload, this data point is the strongest current argument for accelerated AI investment in the close and planning cycle.
**Governance as the Real Gating Factor** Strategic decisions, exception handling, and material approvals still require human judgment, and any credible agentic platform will route these to a human rather than attempting to resolve them autonomously. Finance teams are integrating AI agents by enforcing SOX-ready audit trails, role-based permissions, and human-in-the-loop approvals for material actions. Banks that cannot demonstrate this governance architecture to examiners will face friction on any AI deployment that touches regulatory reporting or capital calculation.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
The single most actionable planning item entering this week: CFOs should stress-test NII guidance under three scenarios from today's jobs print -- a strong number that cements September hike probability above sixty-five percent, a weak number that reopens the hold/cut debate, and a miss that triggers revision of prior months and changes the narrative on labor market health. The unemployment rate remains at four point one percent despite some declines in monthly payroll readings, and Friday's August jobs report remains important in determining the Fed's path.
On transformation, the demand signal is now clearest in two places: regulatory capital model rebuilds required by the Basel re-proposal (driving demand in treasury and risk systems), and the close/FP&A automation build-out where the ROI gap between pilot and enterprise deployment is motivating platform-level purchasing rather than point solutions.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The market and most bank planning teams are treating Warsh's hawkish stance as the dominant scenario and building hike assumptions into Q3 and Q4 NII models. But July payrolls fell by twenty-three thousand and average hourly earnings grew only three point two percent year-over-year, the lowest since May 2021 -- a labor market that is weakening faster than the inflation data suggests. If today's August jobs report shows a second consecutive negative or near-zero print, the September hike probability collapses and every bank CFO who front-ran the hike in NII guidance has re-work to do. The real risk is not getting the rate call wrong; it is having built scenario sets that do not span both sides of a genuinely binary outcome.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **The Basel operational risk flip:** Every super-regional above one-hundred billion dollars now faces a mandatory shift from internal models to the Standardized Approach for operational risk capital -- regardless of whether total capital goes up or down. How is your bank's treasury and risk function rebuilding the calculation infrastructure that the new rule requires, and is your finance transformation roadmap accounting for that implementation timeline?
2. **The agentic AI ROI gap:** Seven percent of CFOs report strong AI impact despite sixty percent running pilots. What is the architectural bottleneck -- data quality, siloed deployment, or governance -- and is your bank's next finance technology dollar going toward fixing the plumbing or adding another pilot?
3. **The jobs-print planning stress test:** With September hike probability at sixty percent and a binary jobs print due today, what is the spread in your NII guidance between the hike and hold scenario -- and is that scenario range being communicated to your board, or is your planning still anchored on a single base case?

item.title: Finance Pulse - Aug 28, 2026
item.description:
I now have sufficient sourced material across all required coverage areas. Let me synthesize the two-part briefing for Friday, August 28, 2026, ensuring every development is genuinely new relative to the prior episode recaps and every claim is anchored.
---
## Finance Pulse | Friday, August 28, 2026
**Bottom line: Today is the day the rate debate either resolves or deepens -- Warsh steps to the podium at ten a.m. ET in Jackson Hole with markets priced roughly seventy percent for a hold in September, September hike odds now down sharply from prior-week peaks, and a Q2 earnings picture for super-regionals that has turned decisively sequential-NII-positive at every institution in the cohort; but the genuinely fresh story today is not the speech itself -- it is the specific structural fact beneath the data: the Warsh-era Fed has traded verbal guidance for deliberate silence, meaning that for the first time since 2022, bank CFOs must build NII scenario models around a chair whose communication philosophy offers fewer anchors, not more, and that shifts the modeling burden squarely onto the finance function's own scenario and sensitivity infrastructure.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. CME FedWatch now shows only thirty percent odds of a September hike, with Goldman Sachs predicting the Fed will hold the federal funds target range at three point fifty to three point seventy-five percent through the remainder of 2026. That is a sharp reversal from the fifty-seven-percent hike odds reported in this series just days ago, and it matters for NII planning immediately.
2. Super-regional banks reported commercial loan growth and higher net interest income in Q2 2026, with net interest income rising sequentially at all eleven banks in the cohort, with Citizens and PNC each up four percent.
3. Net charge-off ratios declined at eight banks, and credit loss allowances fell at ten of eleven institutions, but CRE performance diverged: Citizens cut its CRE charge-off rate to zero point thirty-six percent from zero point sixty-four percent, while Truist, U.S. Bancorp, and KeyCorp each recorded higher CRE nonperforming assets despite overall charge-off declines, suggesting uneven stress from legacy office and multifamily exposure.
4. BCG's June 2026 executive perspectives report finds that with AI agents now able to reason, plan, and execute multi-step finance workflows with limited human input, eighty-eight percent of CFOs now view AI as essential -- and agentic capabilities can fundamentally shift finance's role from a producer of numbers to something more strategic.
5. Bain projects that mergers among regionals will create one to three new megabanks with at least one trillion dollars in assets by 2030, with the ranks of regional banks shrinking from forty-nine to as few as thirty, and Bain explicitly flags M&A to add AI and technology capabilities as a primary driver.
---
### Key Themes
**Theme 1 (New): The Warsh Silence Penalty** Warsh himself described his public language since May as deliberately spare by design, so the FOMC minutes and the dissent count may end up saying more about where the Committee actually stands than the speech itself. Whether Warsh characterizes the next meeting is the crux: the Fed's next rate decision is September sixteenth, and this Fed has largely stopped commenting between meetings, meaning any hint at all about that decision tends to move markets within minutes, and saying nothing is itself a signal that nothing is changing. For bank CFOs, a chair who declines to guide creates a structural gap in NII modeling that only better internal scenario infrastructure can fill.
**Theme 2 (Evolving): Deposit Mix Pressure Inside a Sequential NII Recovery** Truist's updated Q2 outlook captures the tension precisely: net interest income is expected to increase one to one and a half percent in 2026 versus 2025, but that updated outlook reflects continued optimization of less strategic lending portfolios, lower loan spreads, and less favorable deposit mix -- with the forward curve now incorporating a twenty-five basis point hike in September. The NII trajectory is positive but precarious, contingent on deposit mix not deteriorating further.
**Theme 3 (New): The M&A-as-AI-Acquisition Signal** For years, bankers have speculated that two of the three biggest super-regionals -- PNC, U.S. Bancorp, and Truist -- could eventually combine to create a new banking champion; Bain's new model projects one to three new megabanks at or above one trillion dollars by 2030. Already this cycle, Fifth Third absorbed Comerica, Huntington added Veritex and Cadence, and PNC acquired FirstBank of Lakewood -- each of which creates an immediate finance integration and data consolidation challenge that pulls forward transformation spend.
---
### Banking Finance-Function Metrics
The PCE price index increased zero point two percent month-on-month in July, above estimates of zero point one percent, reversing a prior decline; annual inflation rose to three point seven percent versus forecasts of three point six percent. Investors now await Warsh's Jackson Hole speech for further clues, although he is not expected to offer a clear signal on the central bank's September decision.
GDP grew one point five percent in Q2 as initially estimated, while durable goods orders rose one point one percent in July, beating expectations of zero point five percent. A resilient real economy removes the recession backstop that would otherwise constrain a hike, keeping the September decision genuinely binary.
The ten-year Treasury note yield was four point sixty-six percent as of the prior close, up two basis points in twenty-four hours. The thirty-year Treasury bond yield was five point eighteen percent. With the curve positively sloped between two and thirty years, asset-sensitive balance sheets are earning, but the cost of new wholesale funding remains elevated.
U.S. Bancorp's NII has been rising over the past few years; going forward, less deposit migration, relatively lower rates, and stabilizing funding costs will continue to support NII and NIM expansion. Following the successful completion of the 2026 stress test, U.S. Bancorp management plans to increase the quarterly dividend by four percent to fifty-four cents per share in Q3 2026.
On the funding side, high-yield savings accounts are now advertising yields of up to four point ten percent as of August 2026 -- a floor that makes deposit cost relief contingent on the Fed actually cutting, which markets now see as a 2027 story.
---
### Regulatory Radar
The FOMC is not expected to issue a policy statement or make any changes to interest rates at Jackson Hole. The next rate-setting meeting is scheduled for September fifteenth and sixteenth, and the central bank will issue a policy decision and Summary of Economic Projections at the conclusion of that meeting. The new SEP will be the first to embed Warsh's own projections, giving bank CFOs an explicit framework to anchor 2026 and 2027 planning curves.
Senator Warren, in a letter released this week, pointed out that Warsh had before becoming chair asserted that tariffs are not inflationary, and that inflation as measured by PCE remains well above the two point eight percent it was in February 2026, prior to the conflict with Iran. Warren also characterized Warsh's statements that AI could help drive productivity as "optimistic assertions" and used her letter to call on Warsh to use the Jackson Hole speech to address the current economic situation directly. The political pressure on the chair's communications strategy is itself a modeling variable.
With the EU AI Act's high-risk-system obligations having become fully enforceable on August second, 2026, the next ninety days will separate the institutions that built their AI stack properly from those that bolted compliance on at the end. This is a real deadline, not a prospective one, and it already governs agentic systems deployed in controllership, credit, and regulatory reporting.
One risk emerging from AI compliance is what practitioners call "Trust Debt" from unvetted AI-generated code; for the CFO, governance is no longer just about Sarbanes-Oxley -- it is about AI ethics and model validation.
---
### AI in Finance
**Deployment reality versus pipeline:** JPMorgan Chase now runs more than four hundred production AI use cases on an enterprise machine-learning platform processing roughly ten trillion dollars in daily transactions; Goldman Sachs has twelve thousand engineers paired with Devin and Claude-based agents handling accounting, compliance, and operational finance; and Commonwealth Bank reduced fraud losses by twenty percent in the first half of FY2026 using a homegrown agent.
Oracle launched a dedicated agentic banking platform in February 2026, and FIS has shipped its first Anthropic-powered Financial Crimes Agent into pilot deployments at BMO and Amalgamated.
Oracle Financial Services extended its agentic AI platform to corporate banking in April 2026, enabling pre-built AI agents for treasury, trade finance, credit, and lending, automating mission-critical processes to speed decision-making.
**BCG framework for the CFO agenda:** Agentic AI is the top topic in CFO conversations today; with AI agents now able to reason, plan, and execute multi-step finance workflows with limited human input, the question for CFOs in 2026 is no longer whether AI will reshape finance but how fast and at what governance cost.
**Governance as the new differentiator:** Fifty-five percent of CFOs surveyed by Wolters Kluwer are concerned about the loss of human judgment and oversight; the consensus position is that human-in-the-loop is non-negotiable, and while AI can recommend an action, the final decision must remain with the human.
**Where budgets are actually moving:** Half of finance chiefs surveyed by Deloitte's CFO Signals Spotlight report named digital transformation as their foremost priority for 2026, ahead of cash management optimization and capital allocation, based on a survey of two hundred CFOs at North American companies with at least one billion dollars in annual revenue. The six priorities CFOs plan to fund include leveraging digital tools to transform finance operations, going all-in on AI, and embedding AI agents directly into finance workflows. The shift from "pilot" to "embed in workflow" is where vendor contract values are rising.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
The combination of today's data points creates a specific and underappreciated planning problem: traders had fully priced a twenty-five basis point Fed rate hike by December as recently as a week earlier, but it has now shifted to January 2027 -- meaning the rate scenario that sat at the center of every Q3 2026 NII model has just moved out a full quarter. Any bank that built a single base-case rate path rather than a probability-weighted scenario set now has a model that needs rebuilding, not just refreshing.
While hype persists, 2026 is shaping up as the year agentic AI will create scaled transformation in financial services, with a clear gap emerging between market leaders, the chasing pack, and the laggards. 1. CME FedWatch now shows only thirty percent odds of a September hike, with Goldman Sachs predicting the Fed will hold the federal funds target range at three point fifty to three point seventy-five percent through the remainder of 2026. 3. 4. BCG's June 2026 executive perspectives report finds that with AI agents now able to reason, plan, and execute multi-step finance workflows with limited human input, eighty-eight percent of CFOs now view AI as essential -- and agentic capabilities can fundamentally shift finance's role from a producer of numbers to something more strategic.
5. **Theme 2 (Evolving): Deposit Mix Pressure Inside a Sequential NII Recovery** Truist's updated Q2 outlook captures the tension precisely: net interest income is expected to increase one to one and a half percent in 2026 versus 2025, but that updated outlook reflects continued optimization of less strategic lending portfolios, lower loan spreads, and less favorable deposit mix -- with the forward curve now incorporating a twenty-five basis point hike in September. The NII trajectory is positive but precarious, contingent on deposit mix not deteriorating further.
**Theme 3 (New): The M&A-as-AI-Acquisition Signal** For years, bankers have speculated that two of the three biggest super-regionals -- PNC, U.S. Bancorp, and Truist -- could eventually combine to create a new banking champion; Bain's new model projects one to three new megabanks at or above one trillion dollars by 2030. The PCE price index increased zero point two percent month-on-month in July, above estimates of zero point one percent, reversing a prior decline; annual inflation rose to three point seven percent versus forecasts of three point six percent. GDP grew one point five percent in Q2 as initially estimated, while durable goods orders rose one point one percent in July, beating expectations of zero point five percent. A resilient real economy removes the recession backstop that would otherwise constrain a hike, keeping the September decision genuinely binary.
The ten-year Treasury note yield was four point sixty-six percent as of the prior close, up two basis points in twenty-four hours. The thirty-year Treasury bond yield was five point eighteen percent. item.title: Finance Pulse - Aug 27, 2026
item.description:
I now have the live data needed to produce a fully sourced, fresh briefing for Thursday, August 27, 2026. All material is genuinely new or newly confirmed relative to the prior episode recaps. Let me synthesize both parts.
---
## Finance Pulse | Thursday, August 27, 2026
**Bottom line: Yesterday's PCE print resolved one debate and opened another -- headline came in at three point seven percent year over year, a tenth hotter than the Dow Jones consensus, while core held exactly in line at three point three percent for the fourth consecutive month, a four-month plateau that is now the single most important fact for bank CFO scenario planning; but the story entering this morning is not the data itself -- it is what that plateau means for how Warsh frames his Jackson Hole keynote in roughly twenty-four hours, and whether the most consequential new variable in banking finance -- the deepening K-shaped divergence in credit card delinquency -- finally forces provisioning models to separate lower-prime exposure from prime exposure rather than running a single blended reserve rate.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. **PCE printed hotter on the headline, flat on the core.** July headline PCE came in at three point seven percent, one tenth above consensus; core held at three point three percent for the fourth straight month. Four months of near-zero progress on core is the planning anchor for every CFO building a second-half NII scenario. 2. **Warsh speaks tomorrow; the market has already priced neutral.** With sixty-nine percent of fund managers surveyed by Bank of America expecting a neutral tone, a neutral speech is already in asset prices. The surprise risk is asymmetric toward hawkish, especially given Warsh's stated preference for regime reform and his criticism of the 2020 FAIT framework. 3. **Credit card delinquency is bifurcating, not deteriorating uniformly.** The ninety-plus day credit card delinquency rate has risen from seven point six percent in Q3 2022 to twelve point eight percent by Q1 2026 -- but the flow rate into new delinquencies has been stable for nearly two years. This divergence demands separate provisioning treatment by segment, not blended reserve modeling. 4. **Basel III re-proposal comment period closed June eighteenth; the next event is a final rule, potentially by Q4 2026.** The revised March 2026 proposal is expected to modestly lower aggregate capital -- not raise it -- but adds operational complexity that drives finance transformation demand. 5. **Agentic AI is at a production inflection, but an ROI credibility gap persists.** Wolters Kluwer estimates forty-four percent of finance teams will use agentic AI in 2026, yet only seven percent of CFOs in a Gartner survey say AI investments are having a strong impact.
---
### Key Themes
**1. The Core PCE Plateau -- and Its Provisioning Corollary (New)** Four consecutive months at or near three point three percent core PCE is not a trend reversal; it is stagnation at a level one point three percentage points above the Fed's target. For bank CFOs, this means rate-cut scenarios continue to recede, deposit repricing relief remains deferred, and the NII recovery built on fixed-rate loan repricing must do more lifting than funding-cost relief. The new corollary: flat spending data, with real consumer spending flat month over month in July against a zero point four percent gain in June, means the loan-growth assumptions embedded in most H2 2026 plans are now at risk of downward revision.
**2. Warsh's Jackson Hole as a Governance Signal for Bank ALM (Evolving)** Prior episodes covered the speech as a rate-path event. Today's new angle: regardless of whether Warsh signals hike or hold, his stated architecture preferences -- shorter statements, less forward guidance, potential regime reform -- structurally raise the volatility of the Fed's reaction function. That permanently increases the value of scenario-based planning over point-estimate forecasting in bank treasury and FP&A, which is a durable demand signal for planning platform investment.
**3. The K-Shaped Credit Delinquency Divergence as a Finance-Function Forcing Function (New)** The delinquency spread between JPMorgan at two point three percent and Synchrony at four point eight percent is now two hundred fifty basis points -- the widest since 2010. The New York Fed's Q2 2026 data show total household debt declining slightly to eighteen point eight trillion dollars, with flow rates into serious delinquency largely stable, meaning the stock of impaired borrowers grew during tightening and has not yet resolved. This forces a rethink of how banks segment the allowance for credit losses: blended consumer reserve rates overstate stress at prime-focused institutions and understate it at lower-prime-exposed ones.
---
### Banking Finance-Function Metrics
**NIM and Rate Sensitivity:** With core PCE stubbornly at three point three percent and no Fed cut on the horizon before September at the earliest, the fixed-rate loan repricing tailwind remains intact. However, yesterday's flat real consumer spending creates a demand-side brake on new loan origination that limits how much volume can absorb improved pricing.
**Credit and Provisioning:** The New York Fed Q2 report shows total household debt fell by thirteen billion dollars to eighteen point eight trillion dollars, a modest de-leveraging. The thirty-plus day credit card delinquency rate on all commercial bank cards actually declined to two point eight five percent in Q2 2026, the lowest since Q2 2023, suggesting the aggregate headline is less alarming than the stock of severely delinquent accounts built up since 2022 implies. For super-regionals with mixed consumer books, the provisioning signal is nuanced: segment matters more than aggregate.
**Consumer Spending Transmission:** Real consumer spending was flat in July after a zero point four percent gain in June, with most discretionary categories contracting. Restaurant spending was the outlier, up four point six percent. For banks modeling fee income and card transaction volume, July's pullback is an early warning worth watching in August data.
**Capital:** The Basel III Proposal's net direction is a modest capital decrease for most institutions, which should free CET1 -- but the operational complexity of new internal model reassessments, governance frameworks, and capital planning recalibration is a workload driver that cannot be absorbed without either headcount or technology.
---
### Regulatory Radar
Following extensive industry feedback, US regulators re-proposed the Basel III Endgame as the Basel III Proposal on March nineteenth, 2026. Comments were due by June eighteenth, 2026. The comment record is now closed. The March 2026 proposals revisit Basel III Endgame for the largest firms, introduce a separate approach for regional and smaller banks, and revise the GSIB surcharge framework -- and taken together the package lowers capital requirements overall, reduces duplication, and improves the economics of traditional lending. However, the 2026 capital rules also add complexity and will require careful implementation, and to capture the benefits of the updated operational risk framework, banks will need to reassess internal models, governance frameworks, and capital planning processes.
The package also creates new strategic and operational questions for treasury, risk, finance, reporting, and data teams as firms assess the impact of the proposals and prepare for implementation. For a finance transformation consultant, that sentence from PwC is a direct buying signal: every bank treasury and regulatory reporting function now has a rules-driven mandate for process and data investment.
On timing: if regulators release a final rule in Q1, it could be finalized in late 2026, with implementation beginning in 2027.
---
### AI in Finance
The production-versus-pilot gap is the sharpest signal this week. According to Wolters Kluwer, forty-four percent of finance teams will use agentic AI in 2026, representing an increase of over six hundred percent. Yet close to sixty percent of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects, while only seven percent of CFOs say those investments are having a strong impact.
That gap has a structural explanation: the gap stems from architectural limitations -- most finance teams are adding AI inside existing functional lanes, and each system may improve a task but also carries its own data model, workflow logic, and audit trail.
On the vendor side, Oracle Financial Services is embedding AI agents for treasury, trade finance, credit, and lending into an enterprise-class suite for corporate banks. Separately, JPMorgan Chase now runs more than four hundred production AI use cases on an enterprise ML platform processing roughly ten trillion dollars in daily transactions, while Goldman Sachs has twelve thousand engineers paired with AI agents handling accounting, compliance, and operational finance.
For super-regionals, the CFO-agenda connection is direct: finance teams sit on a unique stack of structured data, recurring cycles, and material decisions -- making the function one of the highest-ROI surfaces for agentic AI when the controls hold. But the prerequisite is data hygiene: the most common failure mode is assuming the existing model is clean enough for agent invocation -- it is rarely true on first inspection, and a three-to-six-week model-hygiene pass before scenario-modeling workflows go live is typically required.
The governance question is sharpening: ninety-nine percent of companies plan to put agents into production but only eleven percent have done so, due to implementation challenges related to data, governance, and security. For banks with heightened regulatory scrutiny, that governance gap is a risk, not just a delay.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
**Scenario planning over point estimates.** The Warsh communication regime -- deliberately ambiguous, less forward guidance, shorter statements -- means bank treasurers and FP&A teams operating on a single rate path are building plans on a foundation that the Fed is actively declining to reinforce. The demand signal is for multi-scenario NII modeling capability, not for refining a base case.
**Provisioning segmentation.** The K-shaped delinquency data forces a segmentation rebuild in allowance models. Banks relying on blended consumer reserve rates need to isolate lower-prime portfolios; the New York Fed's own research now provides the academic framing for that conversation with auditors and regulators.
**Basel complexity as a transformation catalyst.** A capital rule that lowers requirements but raises operational complexity is a net positive for finance transformation budgets: it removes the political argument against investment while creating a regulatory mandate for process change. Controllers and risk finance teams at institutions above one hundred billion dollars in assets face the most acute need for model and data infrastructure upgrades.
**AI ROI credibility gap.** With only seven percent of CFOs reporting strong AI impact despite sixty percent piloting, the conversation has shifted from "should we do this" to "why aren't we seeing returns." The answer -- siloed deployment, poor data hygiene, no cross-functional integration -- is precisely the consulting engagement that finance transformation practices are positioned to deliver.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The consensus framing is that a capital-lighter Basel III final rule is unambiguously good for banks. It probably is for ROE. But the operational-complexity increase embedded in the same rule creates a multi-year finance-function workload that most super-regionals have not yet budgeted for. The banks most likely to outperform on capital efficiency post-implementation are the ones investing now in data infrastructure and model governance -- not the ones waiting for a final rule to plan their response. The contrarian bet is that the winners of Basel III relief will be determined by transformation investment decisions made in the next six months, not by the capital math itself.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **"The PCE plateau is your planning anchor -- not the September decision."** Four months of flat core at three point three percent means the rate path has less variance than the FOMC dissent votes suggest. Ask your client: has the FP&A team stress-tested NII under a scenario where rates do not move until Q1 2027?
2. **"Your provisioning model may be lying to you."** The K-shaped delinquency divergence means blended consumer reserve rates systematically misprice risk at both ends of the quality spectrum. Ask: how does your allowance model treat lower-prime card exposure versus prime card exposure, and when was that segmentation last validated against actual flow-into-delinquency data?
3. **"Basel III gives you budget cover for the data work you already needed to do."** The new capital rules lower requirements but raise modeling and governance complexity. For any client that has been deferring a data or reporting infrastructure build, this is the regulatory mandate that makes the business case.

### AI in Finance
The production-versus-pilot gap is the sharpest signal this week. According to Wolters Kluwer, forty-four percent of finance teams will use agentic AI in 2026, representing an increase of over six hundred percent. Yet close to sixty percent of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects, while only seven percent of CFOs say those investments are having a strong impact.
That gap has a structural explanation: the gap stems from architectural limitations -- most finance teams are adding AI inside existing functional lanes, and each system may improve a task but also carries its own data model, workflow logic, and audit trail.
On the vendor side, Oracle Financial Services is embedding AI agents for treasury, trade finance, credit, and lending into an enterprise-class suite for corporate banks. Separately, JPMorgan Chase now runs more than four hundred production AI use cases on an enterprise ML platform processing roughly ten trillion dollars in daily transactions, while Goldman Sachs has twelve thousand engineers paired with AI agents handling accounting, compliance, and operational finance.
For super-regionals, the CFO-agenda connection is direct: finance teams sit on a unique stack of structured data, recurring cycles, and material decisions -- making the function one of the highest-ROI surfaces for agentic AI when the controls hold. But the prerequisite is data hygiene: the most common failure mode is assuming the existing model is clean enough for agent invocation -- it is rarely true on first inspection, and a three-to-six-week model-hygiene pass before scenario-modeling workflows go live is typically required.
The governance question is sharpening: ninety-nine percent of companies plan to put agents into production but only eleven percent have done so, due to implementation challenges related to data, governance, and security. For banks with heightened regulatory scrutiny, that governance gap is a risk, not just a delay.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
**Scenario planning over point estimates.** The Warsh communication regime -- deliberately ambiguous, less forward guidance, shorter statements -- means bank treasurers and FP&A teams operating on a single rate path are building plans on a foundation that the Fed is actively declining to reinforce. The demand signal is for multi-scenario NII modeling capability, not for refining a base case.
**Provisioning segmentation.** The K-shaped delinquency data forces a segmentation rebuild in allowance models. Banks relying on blended consumer reserve rates need to isolate lower-prime portfolios; the New York Fed's own research now provides the academic framing for that conversation with auditors and regulators.
**Basel complexity as a transformation catalyst.** A capital rule that lowers requirements but raises operational complexity is a net positive for finance transformation budgets: it removes the political argument against investment while creating a regulatory mandate for process change. Controllers and risk finance teams at institutions above one hundred billion dollars in assets face the most acute need for model and data infrastructure upgrades.
**AI ROI credibility gap.** With only seven percent of CFOs reporting strong AI impact despite sixty percent piloting, the conversation has shifted from "should we do this" to "why aren't we seeing returns." The answer -- siloed deployment, poor data hygiene, no cross-functional integration -- is precisely the consulting engagement that finance transformation practices are positioned to deliver.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The consensus framing is that a capital-lighter Basel III final rule is unambiguously good for banks. It probably is for ROE. But the operational-complexity increase embedded in the same rule creates a multi-year finance-function workload that most super-regionals have not yet budgeted for. The banks most likely to outperform on capital efficiency post-implementation are the ones investing now in data infrastructure and model governance -- not the ones waiting for a final rule to plan their response. The contrarian bet is that the winners of Basel III relief will be determined by transformation investment decisions made in the next six months, not by the capital math itself.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **"The PCE plateau is your planning anchor -- not the September decision."** Four months of flat core at three point three percent means the rate path has less variance than the FOMC dissent votes suggest. Ask your client: has the FP&A team stress-tested NII under a scenario where rates do not move until Q1 2027?
2. **"Your provisioning model may be lying to you."** The K-shaped delinquency divergence means blended consumer reserve rates systematically misprice risk at both ends of the quality spectrum. Ask: how does your allowance model treat lower-prime card exposure versus prime card exposure, and when was that segmentation last validated against actual flow-into-delinquency data?
3. **"Basel III gives you budget cover for the data work you already needed to do."** The new capital rules lower requirements but raise modeling and governance complexity. For any client that has been deferring a data or reporting infrastructure build, this is the regulatory mandate that makes the business case.

item.title: Finance Pulse - Aug 26, 2026
item.description:
I now have sufficient sourced material to produce today's fully fresh two-part briefing. Let me synthesize it now.
---
## Finance Pulse | Wednesday, August 26, 2026
**Bottom line: Today is the day PCE prints -- the BEA's July release, due this morning, is consensus-pegged at three point six percent headline and three point three percent core, which if it matches would leave the September hike debate precisely unresolved; but the genuinely new story this Wednesday is not the print itself, it is what sits beneath the surface of the July commercial lending data: fixed-rate NIM expanded fourteen basis points in a single month after narrowing for six consecutive months, a reversal that reshapes how CFOs should frame second-half NII guidance, while the Basel III re-proposal's comment record quietly closed in June, moving the rule toward a final phase that will force every bank's treasury, risk, and finance teams to rearchitect capital calculations -- a workload the March 2026 proposals explicitly extended to regional banks for the first time.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. **PCE prints today (August 26):** Economists project that inflation slowed a touch in July, with the PCE price gauge seen climbing three point six percent on a yearly basis; the core reading, which strips out food and energy, is forecast to hold steady at a three point three percent annual pace. If the numbers match those estimates, the debate over whether the Federal Reserve should lift its benchmark interest rate in September will remain unresolved.
2. **Fixed-rate NIM reversal is the most actionable new fact for bank CFOs:** The August analysis of the Q2 PrecisionLender commercial loan and deposit pricing database, covering July 2026 activity, shows the picture is broadly positive for the first time in several months -- spreads expanded across all three rate structures and fixed-rate spreads, which had been narrowing since January, reversed that trend in July for the first time. Fixed NIM rose fourteen basis points, from one point seven zero percent to one point eight four percent, with essentially the full spread expansion flowing through to margin.
3. **Basel III re-proposal now in its final approach -- and regional banks are newly in scope:** The March 2026 proposals revisit Basel III Endgame for the largest firms, introduce a separate approach for regional and smaller banks, and revise the GSIB surcharge framework. Taken together, the package lowers capital requirements overall, reduces duplication across the framework, and improves the economics of traditional lending -- but also creates new strategic and operational questions for treasury, risk, finance, reporting, and data teams as firms assess the impact and prepare for implementation.
---
### Key Themes
**1. The July PCE print as a September pivot moment (New)** A Wednesday release of the PCE index is anticipated to show a three point six percent rise over the twelve months ending in July, based on a Dow Jones Newswires and Wall Street Journal survey of economists -- that would represent a slight cooling from June's three point seven percent annual gain. PCE methodology is set to be revised on September 30 to eliminate the distortion created by portfolio management services prices, which means the September FOMC will be the last one to interpret inflation under the current measurement construct. This is a rarely-discussed planning assumption wrinkle: the metric the Fed is hiking or holding against changes immediately after the September decision.
**2. The fixed-rate NIM reversal -- a genuine mid-year signal (New)** SOFR funding costs have remained relatively stable year-to-date, ending July at four point three five percent, and the divergence between fixed and floating funding costs is one of the more significant structural shifts in the pricing equation this year. For CFOs: the single-month fixed NIM reversal after six months of compression is a material development for second-half NII guidance, but it arrives against a funding curve that keeps steepening -- making the durability of the improvement the core uncertainty.
**3. Agentic AI crossing from pilots to production governance (Evolving)** JPMorgan Chase now runs more than four hundred production AI use cases on an enterprise machine learning platform, and Goldman Sachs has twelve thousand engineers paired with AI agents handling accounting, compliance, and operational finance. The 2026 conversation among banking CIOs is about production architecture, regulatory load-bearing controls, and which functions ship to autonomous agents next -- with the EU AI Act's high-risk-system obligations now fully enforceable as of August 2, 2026.
---
### Banking Finance-Function
**NIM and Funding Costs:** With costs rising but revenue rising faster, NIM improved in July across both deal types; fixed NIM rose fourteen basis points. The Federal Reserve cut short-term rates by seventy-five basis points last fall, but deposit rates in the Q2 PrecisionLender portfolio have not followed that move lower by anything close to that magnitude. The Citizens Financial (CFG) Q2 filing confirms a related pattern: interest-bearing deposit costs outperformed a mid-thirty-percent beta, with the expectation that full-year 2026 net interest income will grow between two point five and four percent, with fixed-rate asset turnover, funding cost management, and loan growth as the key drivers.
**Credit and Provisioning:** At Enterprise Financial, the positive NIM trend was offset by a sharp increase in credit costs -- the provision for credit losses more than doubled to fourteen point two million dollars from seven point two million in Q1, driven by two significant commercial charge-offs occurring late in the period. This pattern -- NIM improving while credit costs spike episodically -- is the core tension in second-half CFO planning.
**Efficiency:** Headline inflation eased to three point four percent year-over-year in July while core inflation fell to two point five percent, giving the labor market enough cover to hold cost structures flat in nominal terms -- but finance functions facing rising regulatory workloads cannot hold headcount flat without automation.
---
### Regulatory Radar
**Basel III Endgame (Evolving -- comment period closed, moving toward finalization):** On March 19, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board, OCC, and FDIC issued three proposals that would comprehensively overhaul the existing U.S. bank capital framework and implement the Basel Committee's 2017 revisions. A primary change in the updated proposal is the removal of the dual-stack framework, where banks calculate capital ratios using both standardized and internal models -- the updated proposal emphasizes a simpler structure to reduce complexity and improve transparency. In the UK, the Prudential Regulation Authority finalized the wider Basel 3.1 package for January 1, 2027, deferring the FRTB Internal Model Approach to January 1, 2028. The jurisdictional divergence is now the dominant implementation planning problem for internationally active banks: rules are live in the UK in 2027, the EU in the same window, and the U.S. timeline remains subject to finalization.
**September 30 PCE Methodology Change:** As noted above, the portfolio management services component of PPI feeds directly into the PCE price index that the Fed targets, and creates misleading swings in reported inflation because higher asset prices mechanically translate into higher prices; PCE methodology is set to be revised on September 30 to eliminate the distortion. Finance teams building Fed-dependent rate path scenarios must account for a one-time measurement shift at that date.
---
### AI in Finance
**Where banks are actually deploying (not piloting):** Oracle launched a dedicated agentic banking platform in February, and FIS has shipped its first Anthropic-powered Financial Crimes Agent into pilot deployments at BMO and Amalgamated. Oracle Financial Services now offers an enterprise-class suite of AI-infused applications and pre-built AI agents for treasury, trade finance, credit, and lending -- automating mission-critical processes and speeding decision-making to help banks navigate market volatility and risk.
**The CFO as buyer:** More than half of CFOs -- fifty-four percent, according to Deloitte's 2026 CFO Signals Survey -- have named integrating AI agents into their finance function as their single biggest digital transformation priority this year. The buying signal is sharpening: finance leaders at major enterprises are no longer asking whether agentic AI belongs in the office of the CFO -- they are asking how fast it can be deployed, which workflows to start with, and what results they should expect.
**Workforce model shift:** Visionaries now anticipate the rise of the "ten-times bank," where a single individual leads a team of AI co-workers to deliver exponentially greater output -- growth is no longer constrained by headcount, but success depends on an organization's ability to reinvent work and shape a human-and-agent workforce, with people remaining in charge of deployment and governance.
**Governance reality check:** The finance chiefs broadly expect AI, including agentic AI, to shift from experimentation to proven, enterprise-wide impact -- but stress that success will depend on factors such as strong governance, clean and trusted data, modernized architectures, and human judgment. For bank finance functions specifically, the EU AI Act enforcement as of August 2 is now the first hard external governance deadline for any AI system classified as high-risk.
**CFO agenda connection:** Every AI deployment in treasury (liquidity forecasting), FP&A (rolling forecasts, scenario planning), and controllership (close automation) is being evaluated against capital allocation pressure. The ROI conversation has shifted from "will it pay back" to "when does it pay back faster than doing nothing while the regulatory workload grows."
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
**The second-half planning reset:** The July fixed-rate NIM reversal, arriving alongside a PCE print that may or may not resolve the September hike question, means CFO planning teams need to run at least three rate scenarios simultaneously through the end of year: hold, plus twenty-five, and hold-then-hike in December. Markets are currently pricing in two twenty-five-basis-point hikes, the first in September and the second in December, followed by no further movement through 2027.
**Basel as a transformation driver:** The regional bank inclusion in the March 2026 re-proposals is the most underappreciated driver of finance transformation demand in the super-regional cohort. Banks have approximately two years to interpret the new rules, assess their impact, address new data and technology needs, and adjust business strategies -- and Basel III Endgame is a chance to modernize capital infrastructure by updating technology, becoming more agile, and addressing inefficiencies to lower operating costs.
**FP&A buying signal:** Real-time visibility has become table stakes -- the new frontier is agentic AI, meaning systems that do not just report on the past but actively simulate the future and recommend actions; one CFO describes this as creating a "digital twin" for the CFO role. Finance platform vendors (OneStream, Oracle EPM, Workday Adaptive) are all racing to embed this framing into their product roadmaps.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The market and most bank CFO communications treat the fixed-rate NIM reversal in July as unambiguously good news. But a one-month reversal after six months of compression, occurring in a month when the funding curve continued to steepen, is as easily explained by temporary competitive pricing relief as by durable structural improvement. July's NIM data point is described by Q2 PrecisionLender analysts as "a positive move at midyear 2026 -- but a single move," with the composition and movement of NIM measures requiring continued monitoring. CFOs who use July as validation for optimistic H2 NII guidance are building on a one-data-point foundation. The more conservative framing -- one reversal in a six-month deteriorating trend -- is the one that protects credibility if August data reverts.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **"How does your NII forecast change if July's fixed-rate NIM reversal is structural versus one-month noise -- and do you have separate scenarios for each?"** 2. **"The March 2026 Basel re-proposal explicitly brings regionals into scope for the first time. Has your finance and risk data infrastructure been assessed against what that means for your capital calculation and reporting build?"** 3. **"The PCE methodology changes on September 30 -- the same month as the FOMC meeting. Are your rate-path planning assumptions built on the pre- or post-revision inflation construct, and does your Fed watcher know which one the FOMC will be using to make the September decision?"**

item.title: Finance Pulse - Aug 25, 2026
item.description:
I now have all the material I need. Let me synthesize a fully sourced, fresh briefing for Tuesday, August 25, 2026.
---
## Finance Pulse | Tuesday, August 25, 2026
**Bottom line: With PCE dropping Wednesday and Warsh at the podium Friday, the week ahead is the last chance for data to settle CFO planning assumptions before the September sixteen FOMC decision -- but the new and underappreciated story is not the rate path itself, it is a deposit-pricing anomaly that has now persisted long enough to be structural: bank deposit costs are not following the Fed's prior seventy-five basis points of cuts lower, leaving CFOs caught between a funding floor that refuses to budge and a NIM recovery that is real but fragile, with the Q2 PrecisionLender data and PNC's own ten-Q now providing the clearest articulation yet of that tension.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. PCE consensus for Wednesday, August 26, is plus zero point one percent month-over-month, with the annual rate forecast to ease from three point seven to three point six percent -- the last major data input before Warsh speaks and before CFOs must finalize their September-rate-scenario weights. 2. PNC's Q2 2026 10-Q, filed this month, is the most specific public articulation of a super-regional CFO's baseline planning assumption: hold at three point five to three point seven five percent through 2026 and into 2027, with NII guided up fifteen to fifteen point five percent full-year versus 2025. 3. The Q2 PrecisionLender data reveals that deposit costs have not followed the Fed's prior cuts lower -- a structural repricing gap that the industry has not fully reconciled in its forward NII models, and that represents the most underexplored friction in finance function scenario planning right now. 4. The Jackson Hole symposium theme, "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy," is a direct setup for the CFO technology and AI agenda, not just a rates story; Warsh's structural framing at the podium will set the vocabulary for the next wave of regulatory guidance on payments modernization and digital rails. 5. TD Securities, in a note circulated this week, explicitly warns Warsh's "ideological reluctance to provide guidance" means the speech is unlikely to resolve September uncertainty -- which itself is an ALM planning fact, not just a market observation.
---
### Key Themes
**Theme 1 (New): The Deposit-Cost Floor Is Not Behaving as Modeled**
The Federal Reserve cut short-term rates by seventy-five basis points last fall, but deposit rates in the Q2 PrecisionLender commercial loan and deposit pricing database have not followed that move lower, at least not by anything close to that magnitude, even as loan activity runs at elevated levels. Spreads did expand across all three rate structures in July, coupons rose in tandem, and NIM improved on both fixed and floating deals -- but July was also notable for the fixed side specifically, where fixed-rate spreads had been narrowing since January and July marked the first month to reverse that trend, while the funding curve continued to steepen, keeping upward pressure on fixed-rate funding costs even as bankers managed to push revenue higher.
This is the new frame: NIM expansion is real but it is being achieved by pushing loan yields faster than deposit costs are declining, not by repricing deposits down. CFOs who modeled a symmetric deposit beta on the cut cycle are now holding the wrong assumption. The finance function implication is direct: scenario models, transfer pricing frameworks, and ALM stress tests all need to be rerun against a higher-for-longer deposit cost floor, even in a hold-or-cut rate environment.
**Theme 2 (Evolving): PNC's 10-Q Gives the Clearest Super-Regional Planning Baseline**
PNC's baseline forecast in its Q2 2026 10-Q is for the Federal Reserve to keep the federal funds rate unchanged throughout 2026 and into 2027, in the three point fifty to three point seventy-five percent range, with risks skewed toward tighter monetary policy given persistent above-target inflation and inflationary pressures from higher energy prices and continued strength in capital spending. For Q3 2026 versus Q2, PNC guides average loans up one to two percent, NII up three to three point five percent, fee income down five to five point five percent, and noninterest expense excluding integration costs down two to three percent. Full-year 2026 guidance versus 2025 calls for NII up fifteen to fifteen point five percent and total revenue up approximately fourteen percent. That combination of double-digit NII growth alongside a hold-rate baseline is the competitive bar every super-regional finance function is now benchmarking against internally.
**Theme 3 (New): Jackson Hole's Official Theme Is a Quiet Signal for Finance Technology Spend**
This year's symposium theme is "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy," with roughly one hundred twenty central bankers, economists, and officials from more than seventy countries attending. There will be valuable insights into the evolving nature of fintech in a world in which agentic AI may at some point need payment rails to enable independent financial decisions. This is not coincidental. Whatever Warsh says about payments modernization and policy at Jackson Hole will become the reference point regulators and supervisors cite when engaging bank treasury and technology teams on real-time payments readiness, instant liquidity reporting, and digital-rail compliance -- all of which run through the finance function.
---
### Banking Finance-Function Metrics
The deposit cost story has a specific data point worth anchoring: Seacoast Banking's Q2 2026 presentation shows cost of deposits at one point five three percent in Q2 2026, down from one point eighty percent in Q2 2025, even as the fed funds upper limit moved from four point fifty to three point seventy-five percent over that period. That is a compression of roughly twenty-seven basis points in deposit costs against a seventy-five basis point Fed cut -- a deposit beta on the cut side of well under forty percent, consistent with the Q2 PrecisionLender finding that costs are sticky.
Columbia Banking's Q2 2026 NIM expanded eighteen basis points year over year to three point ninety-three percent, with the cost of interest-bearing deposits declining fifty-six basis points to one point ninety-six percent and total deposit costs falling from one point seventy-three to one point thirty-two percent. That is one of the wider deposit repricing moves in the regional cohort, suggesting the mix shift toward noninterest-bearing deposits is doing significant work. Management expects the margin to reach or exceed four percent in Q3, supported by continued loan repricing, a shift toward higher-return relationship lending, and reductions in higher-cost funding.
On credit: Enterprise Financial's Q2 2026 results showed solid NIM expansion and loan growth overshadowed by elevated credit costs, with two large commercial charge-offs totaling approximately fourteen million dollars driving net income to forty million dollars, or one dollar and nine cents per diluted share, down from one dollar and thirty cents in the prior quarter. The credit normalization story is now the governor on NIM-driven optimism across the regional space.
Truist posted a fifteen point four percent ROTCE this quarter, while Citizens Financial guided full-year 2026 NII growth of two point five to four percent, with interest-bearing deposit costs outperforming mid-thirties-percent beta and an increasing noninterest-bearing deposit mix.
---
### Regulatory Radar
Basel III Endgame: no new finalization announcement this week; the story remains the March 2026 re-proposal. The March 2026 proposals revisit Basel III Endgame for the largest firms, introduce a separate approach for regional and smaller banks, and revise the GSIB surcharge framework; they follow a broader review that also produced proposed stress testing changes and recently finalized leverage changes; taken together, the package lowers capital requirements overall, reduces duplication, and improves the economics of traditional lending, but also creates new strategic and operational questions for treasury, risk, finance, reporting, and data teams as firms assess impact and prepare for implementation. Comment period closed June eighteen; the next material event is finalization, expected by Q4 2026 with implementation beginning 2027. The finance function implication: the data and technology requirements embedded in the final rule are what drive transformation spend, regardless of the aggregate capital outcome.
---
### AI in Finance
The most actionable new signal this week is the sequencing pattern now visible across enterprise deployments. Across organizations deploying agentic AI in production finance operations, AP automation typically deploys first due to high volume, clear rules, and measurable baseline metrics; reconciliation and close automation follows as AP success builds organizational confidence; FP&A forecast refresh automates once operational data quality improves through AP and close automation; AR collections automate last due to external data dependencies and customer-facing considerations -- and each phase builds data quality, organizational capability, and governance infrastructure that the next phase depends on, with organizations that skip steps typically facing regression and remediation costs.
This sequencing is the buying signal for bank finance technology decisions. Banks that are still in AP automation pilots are eighteen to thirty-six months from FP&A agentic deployment, because the data plumbing has to be right first.
The ROI gap is the central governance issue. Gartner predicts ninety percent of finance functions will deploy at least one AI-enabled technology solution by 2026, yet close to sixty percent of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects while only seven percent of CFOs say those investments are having a strong impact -- a gap that stems from architectural limitations.
For the controller specifically: the controller becomes the disposition authority on agent-flagged items, which raises the importance of the controller's analytical depth as dispositions get sampled at audit; the FP&A lead becomes the quality-of-output owner for agent-generated artifacts; and the CFO retains sign-off authority on board-pack narratives and close memos -- the agent does not change the sign-off, only the draft cycle that produces what gets signed.
A new role is crystallizing in mature programs. A finance agent owner, often sitting under the controller or FP&A lead, is responsible for prompt curation, eval maintenance, model-update review, and the evidence pipeline -- a role that does not exist in traditional finance org charts, with teams that try to absorb the work into existing roles often seeing it deprioritized under cycle pressure; the right move is a named role with a defined fraction of the week dedicated to agent program quality. Banks should be asking whether that role is in their headcount plan.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
The pre-Jackson Hole data calendar is the immediate CFO action item. The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes July PCE on Wednesday, August 26 at eight thirty a.m. Eastern, alongside the second estimate of Q2 GDP -- headline PCE consensus is plus zero point one percent month-over-month, core PCE plus zero point two percent with the annual rate holding at three point three percent.
